content: Neonatal sepsis is a significant contributor to both illness and death in newborns, ranking as the third leading cause of neonatal mortality worldwide and accounting for 13% of all neonatal deaths. Despite the substantial burden posed by neonatal sepsis, there is a notable lack of high-quality evidence regarding its diagnosis and treatment. The diagnostic challenges associated with sepsis, combined with the relative immunosuppression of neonates, result in many newborns receiving antibiotics for suspected sepsis. Antibiotics are now the most frequently used medications in neonatal intensive care units. Observational studies conducted in high-income countries indicate that 83% to 94% of neonates treated with antibiotics for suspected sepsis have negative blood cultures. The last Cochrane Review on this topic was updated in 2005, highlighting the need for a more recent systematic review to evaluate the effects of various antibiotic regimens for late-onset neonatal sepsis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of different antibiotic regimens for late-onset neonatal sepsis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple electronic databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase Ovid, CINAHL, LILACS, and the Science Citation Index EXPANDED, as well as clinical trial registries and reference lists of relevant articles. The search was completed on March 12, 2021. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared different antibiotic regimens for late-onset neonatal sepsis. Eligible participants were neonates older than 72 hours at the time of randomization, with suspected or confirmed diagnoses of neonatal sepsis, meningitis, osteomyelitis, endocarditis, or necrotizing enterocolitis. Trials focusing on fungal infections were excluded. Three independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. The GRADE approach was used to determine the certainty of the evidence. The primary outcome of interest was all-cause mortality, while secondary outcomes included serious adverse events, respiratory support, circulatory support, nephrotoxicity, neurological developmental impairment, necrotizing enterocolitis, and ototoxicity. The primary time point for analysis was the maximum follow-up period. The review included five RCTs involving a total of 580 participants. All five trials were determined to have a high risk of bias and provided evidence of very low certainty. Each trial evaluated a different comparison of antibiotic regimens. Specifically, one trial compared cefazolin plus amikacin with vancomycin plus amikacin; another compared ticarcillin plus clavulanic acid with flucloxacillin plus gentamicin; a third compared cloxacillin plus amikacin with cefotaxime plus gentamicin; a fourth compared meropenem with standard care (ampicillin plus gentamicin or cefotaxime plus gentamicin); and the fifth compared vancomycin plus gentamicin with vancomycin plus aztreonam. None of the five trials demonstrated any significant differences in outcomes such as all-cause mortality, serious adverse events, circulatory support, nephrotoxicity, neurological developmental impairment, or necrotizing enterocolitis. However, none of the trials had a sufficient sample size to provide robust evidence regarding the comparative benefits and risks of any specific antibiotic regimen. Additionally, none of the trials assessed respiratory support or ototoxicity. Due to the lack of relevant data, a meta-analysis could not be performed. The lack of well-powered trials and the high risk of systematic errors mean that the benefits and harms of different antibiotic regimens for late-onset neonatal sepsis remain unclear. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to determine whether any particular antibiotic regimen is superior for the treatment of late-onset neonatal sepsis. There is a pressing need for well-designed RCTs with low risks of bias to evaluate the comparative effectiveness and safety of different antibiotic regimens in this population.
